title: The Poincaré Ball Has Room for Your Tree

body:
A balanced binary tree of depth $d$ has $2^{d+1}-1$ nodes. If you try to lay those nodes out in Euclidean space so that graph distance between nodes matches Euclidean distance between their embeddings, you run out of room almost immediately. The volume of a Euclidean ball of radius $r$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ grows polynomially in $r$. The number of tree nodes within graph distance $r$ of the root grows exponentially in $r$. Two shapes of growth, one trying to contain the other: the embedding must either collapse distances or distort them.

Hyperbolic space does not have this problem. In the hyperbolic plane $\mathbb{H}^2$, the circumference of a geodesic circle of radius $r$ grows like $2\pi \sinh r$, i.e. exponentially. The hyperbolic plane has, in a precise sense, enough room to lay a tree out without crushing it. In 2017 Maximilian Nickel and Douwe Kiela turned this geometric observation into a representation-learning method: embed symbolic data into the Poincaré ball, train with Riemannian SGD, enjoy the volume-growth tailwind. Nearly a decade on, the hyperbolic literature has grown into deep architectures, surveys and a careful counter-literature on when the geometry actually pays off. The ingredients are worth having in hand even if your current project embeds nothing hierarchical, because they turn up everywhere hierarchy does.

## Why this matters

Lexical taxonomies, phylogenetic trees, directory structures, citation graphs, legal case law, species classifications, ontologies in biomedicine — hierarchy is a standing feature of symbolic data, and the standard answer in NLP for a long time has been "embed in $\mathbb{R}^n$ with enough dimensions and pretend". That answer works less well than one might hope. Even on an easy tree, Euclidean embeddings pay for the volume mismatch with distortion that balloons with depth. On WordNet, the hyperbolic answer gets to a mean-average-precision of 0.989 at *two* dimensions. Two. For a representation geometer, that is the kind of number that forces an explanation.

The explanation is the geometry, not the parameter count. If a problem is tree-shaped, a tree-shaped space is a better container than a flat one. The practical question is: which problems really are tree-shaped, and when does that structure survive the training objective? Both halves have had answers sharpen in the last two years. There is also a reason the material belongs in a working ML toolkit even outside overtly hierarchical tasks: interpretability work on language models repeatedly finds that semantic directions are closer to tree-ordered than feature-ordered, and hyperbolic geometry is where tree order lives natively. If one wants a prior that respects "is-a" relations without hard-coding them into a loss, this is the geometry that does it for free.

## The core idea

Fix an open unit ball $\mathbb{B}^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : \|x\| < 1\}$ and endow it with the Riemannian metric

$$ g_x \;=\; \left(\frac{2}{1-\|x\|^2}\right)^{2} g^E, $$

where $g^E$ is the Euclidean metric. This is the **Poincaré ball** model of $n$-dimensional hyperbolic space $\mathbb{H}^n$ at constant curvature $-1$. The conformal factor blows up near the boundary, which is why distances in $\mathbb{B}^n$ grow much faster than they look to a Euclidean eye. Explicitly, the induced distance is

$$ d_{\mathbb{B}}(x, y) \;=\; \operatorname{arcosh}\!\left(1 + 2 \,\frac{\|x-y\|^2}{(1-\|x\|^2)(1-\|y\|^2)}\right). $$

A point one Euclidean millimetre from the boundary is hyperbolically far from a point in the middle; a tiny Euclidean displacement near the boundary is a long hyperbolic step. This is the mechanism that lets a disc contain a tree.

A sharpened version of the exponential-growth intuition is **Sarkar's construction**: any tree can be embedded combinatorially into the two-dimensional Poincaré disc so that every pairwise graph distance is reproduced up to multiplicative factor $1+\varepsilon$, with no optimisation. Place the root at the origin; place each node's children on a hyperbolic circle of radius $\tau$ around it, with children spaced in angle to give each subtree its own cone. Recurse. As the scale $\tau$ grows (and the embedding spreads toward the boundary), the distortion goes to zero. Sala, De Sa, Gu and Ré generalised this to the Poincaré ball $\mathbb{B}^d$ and traced the full precision–dimension tradeoff.

Representation learning adds two more ingredients. One is a Riemannian optimiser. The Euclidean gradient $\nabla^E \mathcal{L}(x)$ is not the right update direction on a curved manifold; it needs to be converted to a Riemannian gradient and then transported along a geodesic. For the Poincaré ball the conversion is especially simple because the metric is conformal: $\nabla^{\mathbb{B}} \mathcal{L}(x) = \big((1-\|x\|^2)/2\big)^{2}\, \nabla^E \mathcal{L}(x)$. The update follows the exponential map at $x$, which for the Poincaré ball reduces to a closed-form **Möbius addition**: $x \oplus v = \big((1+2\langle x,v\rangle + \|v\|^2)x + (1-\|x\|^2)v\big)/\big(1 + 2\langle x,v\rangle + \|x\|^2\|v\|^2\big)$. In practice this is Riemannian SGD with a projection step that keeps iterates inside the ball; the whole optimiser fits in a dozen lines. The key subtlety is the step-size scaling near the boundary — a nominal learning rate of $\eta$ corresponds to a hyperbolic step of $\eta \cdot 2/(1-\|x\|^2)^2$, which blows up as $x$ nears the edge and is where most numerical failures start.

The other ingredient is a loss. Nickel and Kiela used a soft nearest-neighbour objective: for each positive edge $(u, v)$ in the hierarchy and a set of negatives $\mathcal{N}(u)$ sampled from non-neighbours,

$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) \;=\; -\sum_{(u,v)} \log \frac{\exp(-d_{\mathbb{B}}(u,v))}{\sum_{v' \in \{v\} \cup \mathcal{N}(u)} \exp(-d_{\mathbb{B}}(u,v'))}. $$

Points on the same branch are pulled close; off-branch points are pushed to the boundary where there is room. In two dimensions this already outperforms Euclidean embeddings on WordNet by a sizeable margin.

Later work prefers the **Lorentz** model — hyperbolic space embedded as one sheet of a hyperboloid in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ — for numerical reasons. Nickel and Kiela's 2018 ICML paper traces the ill-conditioning of the Poincaré distance near the boundary, moves to the hyperboloid, and reports cleaner optimisation. Ganea, Bécigneul and Hofmann built *hyperbolic neural networks* on top: hyperbolic analogues of linear layers, logistic regression and GRUs, all working through the Möbius gyrovector-space formalism. Chen et al.'s *Fully Hyperbolic Neural Networks* (ACL 2022) argues further that staying in the Lorentz model throughout — rather than ferrying each operation out to a tangent space, doing a Euclidean linear map, and ferrying back — gives better expressive power, because Lorentz transformations include boosts the tangent-space detour drops.

## A concrete anchor

Picture a complete binary tree of depth $4$: $31$ nodes. In the Poincaré disc $\mathbb{B}^2$, place the root at the origin and apply Sarkar's rule with scale $\tau = 1$. Each of the root's two children sits on the hyperbolic circle of radius $1$ around the origin, which Euclideanly is a circle of radius $\tanh(1/2) \approx 0.46$. Their children sit on hyperbolic circles of radius $1$ around *them*, which Euclideanly is much closer to the boundary, around $0.75$. One more level and the leaves are at Euclidean radius $\approx 0.92$, hyperbolically four units out.

The leaves of two different subtrees that are graph-distance $8$ apart really are hyperbolic-distance $\approx 8$ apart in the embedding; their Euclidean distance is close to the diameter of the disc, around $1.8$. No optimisation, no learning: the geometry does the work. If you repeat the exercise in $\mathbb{R}^2$ you cannot keep both the depth and the breadth separations; the leaves of adjacent subtrees crowd each other, and distortion grows with depth. Hyperbolic space pays no such tax.

## What it implies in practice

Three handles the geometry gives you for everyday work. First, if your embedding target has even an approximate tree structure, try hyperbolic in low dimension before piling parameters into a Euclidean one. The Poincaré-ball WordNet result at $n=2$ is not an isolated trick: a reasonable prior is that low-dimensional hyperbolic baselines will outperform low-dimensional Euclidean ones whenever the data has latent hierarchy, which is often enough to warrant a diagnostic run. Second, if you already have Euclidean embeddings and want to know whether a hyperbolic recasting might help, estimate the **Gromov $\delta$-hyperbolicity** of your data's metric structure: trees are $0$-hyperbolic, well-behaved tree-like metrics have small $\delta$ relative to the diameter, and genuinely non-hyperbolic data has $\delta$ comparable to the diameter. Third, if you fit a hyperbolic model and the embedded points cluster near the origin rather than spreading toward the boundary, the geometry is not doing anything your data cares about and you have paid in Riemannian optimisation overhead for a Euclidean answer; that is a diagnostic, not a success.

## Limits and open questions

The core caveat is unglamorous: a lot of data is not hyperbolic. Hyperbolic deep-learning surveys through 2024 record genuine wins in few-shot learning, hierarchical image classification, graph tasks on tree-like networks, and knowledge-graph embedding — and genuine draws or losses on dense Euclidean-friendly tasks. Yang et al. (ICML 2023) sharpen the complaint: the field has quietly assumed that if you fit a hyperbolic model with Riemannian optimisation the hierarchy will self-organise, when in fact nothing in the usual objective enforces it, and real embeddings often fail to use the manifold's curvature at all.

Numerical issues are real. The Poincaré distance's $\operatorname{arcosh}$ argument blows up near the boundary and the gradient scales with $(1-\|x\|^2)^2$; standard practice is clipping, the Lorentz reformulation, or custom numerically stable formulas. Mixing curvatures across layers is unresolved: there is no settled theory of how to compose spaces with different signatures. And the engineering baseline is strong — modern Euclidean transformers trained on enough data learn hierarchy by brute force, and at that scale the question becomes whether the geometric prior repays its complexity. The honest answer in late 2026 is: in low dimension and on tree-shaped data, yes; past that, the case has to be made per task.

## Further reading

- Nickel, M. and Kiela, D. (2017). *Poincaré Embeddings for Learning Hierarchical Representations.* NeurIPS 2017. <https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2017/hash/59dfa2df42d9e3d41f5b02bfc32229dd-Abstract.html>. The paper that put hyperbolic embeddings on the ML map; the two-dimensional WordNet result is here.
- Nickel, M. and Kiela, D. (2018). *Learning Continuous Hierarchies in the Lorentz Model of Hyperbolic Geometry.* ICML 2018 (PMLR vol. 80, pp. 3779–3788). <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/nickel18a.html>. The move from the Poincaré ball to the Lorentz model, and why that matters numerically.
- Sala, F., De Sa, C., Gu, A. and Ré, C. (2018). *Representation Tradeoffs for Hyperbolic Embeddings.* ICML 2018 (PMLR vol. 80, pp. 4460–4469). <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v80/sala18a.html>. Precision–dimension tradeoff bounds, Sarkar's construction extended to $\mathbb{B}^d$, and hyperbolic MDS.
- Ganea, O., Bécigneul, G. and Hofmann, T. (2018). *Hyperbolic Neural Networks.* NeurIPS 2018. <https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2018/hash/dbab2adc8f9d078009ee3fa810bea142-Abstract.html>. Möbius gyrovector operations and the first full hyperbolic deep-learning stack.
- Chen, W., Han, X., Lin, Y., Zhao, H., Liu, Z., Li, P., Sun, M. and Zhou, J. (2022). *Fully Hyperbolic Neural Networks.* ACL 2022, pp. 5672–5686. <https://aclanthology.org/2022.acl-long.389>. Argues for staying in the Lorentz model throughout rather than tangent-space detours.
- Yang, M., Verma, H., Zhang, D. C., Liu, J., King, I. and Ying, R. (2023). *Hyperbolic Representation Learning: Revisiting and Advancing.* ICML 2023 (PMLR vol. 202). <https://proceedings.mlr.press/v202/yang23u.html>. The sharpest contemporary critique of the implicit assumption that hyperbolic training automatically preserves hierarchy.
- Mettes, P., Atigh, M. G., Keller-Ressel, M., Gu, J. and Yeung, S. (2024). *Hyperbolic Deep Learning in Computer Vision: A Survey.* IJCV. <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11263-024-02043-5>. A current, careful map of where the geometry pays off and where it does not.
